propositions.text: Claimant is an Albanian citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA sections 96, 97(1)(a), and 97(1)(b).
propositions.quote: XXXXX XXXXX is a citizen of Albania. He claims for refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96, 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant is an Albanian citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA sections 96, 97(1)(a), and 97(1)(b).

propositions.text: Claimant alleges birth in Albania and family migration to the USA in 1988 with green cards.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he was born in Albania and that, in 1988, accompanied by his family, he went to the United States of America (USA) where his family and he were given their green cards.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges he was born in Albania and migrated with family to the USA in 1988, receiving green cards.

propositions.text: In 2004 in Michigan, claimant and friends fought to help his best friend attacked by a disputing individual and his friends.
propositions.quote: In XXXXX 2004, the claimant was with his friends in, Michigan, when his best friend, XXXXX XXXXX, was attacked by an individual with whom he had dispute. That person was also accompanied by his friends when they attacked XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant and his friends went to help XXXXX XXXXX and everyone present got into a fight.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges a 2004 fight in Michigan defending his best friend from attackers.

propositions.text: Three days later, claimant and friends were shot at by attackers; claimant was shot and his friend died from wounds.
propositions.quote: Three days later, the claimant and his friends were confronted by three individuals who were part of the group who had fought with them earlier. They had weapons with which they began shooting at the claimant and his friends. The claimant was shot in his XXXXX XXXXX. His friend, XXXXX, was also shot; he later died because of the bullet wound.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges he and friends were shot at days later; he was wounded and his friend died.

propositions.text: Shooters were Albanian criminals; one arrested, two not; claimant reported and testified, leading to blood feud declared against him.
propositions.quote: The individuals who had shot XXXXX were criminals from Albania. One of the persons was arrested by the police at the scene but the two were not. Because the claimant made a police report and testified against the three individuals, the families of the individuals declared a blood feud against the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges the shooters were Albanian criminals; after his testimony, their families declared a blood feud against him.

propositions.text: Blood feud caused claimant's sister to flee, family sold home; claimant became addicted to marijuana, caught for trafficking in 2006, and deported to Albania in 2008.
propositions.quote: As a result of the blood feud, the claimant's sister fled from California and his family sold their home. The claimant got addicted to marijuana thereafter. In 2006, he was caught and implicated by the police for being in possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking. In XXXXX 2008, the claimant was detained by the immigration authorities and was deported to Albania.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges blood feud consequences, drug addiction, trafficking arrest in 2006, and deportation to Albania in 2008.

propositions.text: In 2009, claimant learned armed people broke into family home intending to kill him; reconciliation efforts failed; he fled to Canada.
propositions.quote: On XXXXX, 2009, upon his arrival in Albania, his father's friend informed him that his neighbours had seen armed people break into his family home in XXXXX. These individuals were waiting to kill him. In XXXXX 2008, his mother's brother in Greece went to seek help from the National Reconciliation Committee to end the blood feud. His efforts did not settle the blood feud and, as a result, the claimant decided to flee to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges armed threats at family home in Albania, failed reconciliation, and flight to Canada.

propositions.text: The key issue is exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this claim is exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies exclusion under Article 1F(b) as the determinative issue.

propositions.text: Article 1F(b) excludes persons with serious non-political crimes outside the refuge country before admission as refugee.
propositions.quote: Article 1(F) reads in part as follows: The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any persons with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (b) The claimant has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee;

paragraphs.summary: The court states Article 1F(b) excludes persons who committed serious non-political crimes outside the refuge country before admission.

propositions.text: UN Handbook defines serious crime as capital or grave punishable act for exclusion under 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The United Nations Handbook1 defines "serious crime" as a capital crime or a grave punishable act. For the purpose of exclusion under I F(b), this serious crime to have been committed by an applicant "outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee".

propositions.text: Exclusion under 1F(b) aims to protect receiving country from refugees who committed serious common crimes before entry.
propositions.quote: The aim of this exclusion clause is to protect the community of the receiving country from the danger of admitting a refugee who has committed serious common crime.

propositions.text: Exclusion under 1F(b) is limited to serious crimes committed before entry into the refuge state, here Canada.
propositions.quote: Exclusion in 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention is limited to "serious crimes" committed before entry into the state of refuge.2 In this case the state of refuge is Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains UN Handbook and precedent define serious crime and exclusion under 1F(b) as protecting Canada from serious crimes committed before entry.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal suggests serious non-political crime means max sentence 10+ years if committed in Canada; this is sensible and followed by Federal Court Trial Division.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal has indicated, without explicitly deciding, that a serious non-political crime should be equated with one in which a maximum sentence of 10 years or more could have been imposed had the crime been committed in Canada. This approach has been characterized as "sensible" and has been followed in the Federal Court Trial Division.3

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Federal Court of Appeal equating serious crime with max 10+ year sentence if committed in Canada, a sensible approach.

propositions.text: Claimant is a compulsive criminal with a US criminal record, deported and lost US permanent resident status; evidence confirms criminal history and illegal entry to Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant in this case is a compulsive criminal. He admitted that he has a criminal record in the USA. Because of the criminal record, he was deported from the USA to Albania and he lost his Permanent Resident status in the USA. Documentary evidence4 is consistent with the claimant's testimony, in that, it confirms that he has a history of criminality in the United States. Moreover, after he lost his status in the USA he entered Canada illegally using his USA Permanent Residence card which was not valid.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant has a US criminal record, was deported, lost US status, and entered Canada illegally.

propositions.text: Claimant committed serious non-political crimes before entering Canada; US reports show multiple marijuana possession and sales in 2006.
propositions.quote: The claimant has committed serious non-political crimes prior to entering Canada. The Incident/Prosecution Reports5 from the USA indicate that, on or about XXXXX, 2006, the claimant had in his possession five to six pounds of marijuana. He was caught selling one pound of marijuana to a customer for $1,400.00. On XXXXX, 2006 he was caught again while he sold 200 grams of Marijuana for $1,000.00. On XXXXX, 2006, he was caught for the third time selling 442 grams, 5.4 grams which he said was for his personal use, and one pound of marijuana in a cereal box for $1,400.00. On XXXXX, 2006, for the fourth time, he was caught selling marijuana in a two gallon size zip lock bag for $3,900.00. He indicated that the two gallons of marijuana was of superior quality and, as a result, was worth more money. He was arrested by an undercover police officer and was detained.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant committed serious non-political crimes before Canada entry, with multiple marijuana sales in 2006.

propositions.text: Claimant convicted of aggravated felony related to drug trafficking and conspiracy in USA, pleaded guilty, sentenced to two years probation, discharged under Youth Trainee Status.
propositions.quote: His testimony and documentary evidence6 indicates that he was convicted of an aggravated felony related to the illicit trafficking in a controlled substance, a conspiracy or attempt to violate law or regulation of a state in the USA and maintaining a drug house. He indicated that, at the hearing, he was represented by a legal counsel who was retained by his family. He indicated that he pleaded guilty to all the charges against him and, as a result, he was convicted and sentence to two years probation on XXXXX, 2008. He was discharged from the two-year probation under Youth Trainee Status.7

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant was convicted of drug trafficking-related aggravated felony, pleaded guilty, sentenced to probation, and discharged under Youth Trainee Status.

propositions.text: Claimant was detained by immigration police, held eight months, deported to Albania, and lost US permanent resident status.
propositions.quote: He indicated that, soon after he was convicted, he was taken from his home by the immigration police. He was placed in immigration detention and was tried by the immigration courts. He testified that he was in detention for about eight months after which he was deported to Albania. He testified that he lost his Permanent Resident status in the USA after he was deported from that country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant was detained by immigration, held eight months, deported, and lost US permanent resident status.

propositions.text: Under Canadian Criminal Code, possession or trafficking of marijuana over 30 grams can lead to max five years jail; multiple offenses could lead to life imprisonment.
propositions.quote: Each time the claimant committed the aforementioned drug-related crime in Canada he would be tried and punished under Section 5, subsection 4 of the Canadian Criminal Code. Under Sections 5(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Criminal Code, he would have been liable for imprisonment for life. According to the documentary evidence provided by the claimant's counsel,8 section 4(1) indicates that each time a person is in possession of more than 30 grams of marijuana or hashish he is punishable to a maximum of five years of jail term. In this case, the claimant was caught on four occasions while being in possession of marijuana over 30 grams. The same documentary evidence indicates that the punishment for trafficking in marijuana or possession for the purpose of trafficking up to 3 kgs in marijuana is up to five years of jail term. In this case, the claimant was caught trafficking in marijuana on four occasions.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Canadian law punishes marijuana possession/trafficking over 30 grams with up to five years jail; multiple offenses could lead to life imprisonment.

propositions.text: Claimant caught four times trafficking marijuana as adult, cumulatively liable for over 10 years jail, thus committed serious crimes in USA before Canada entry.
propositions.quote: Therefore, based on the evidence adduced, since the claimant was an adult and was caught on four occasions to be in possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking, he is cumulatively liable for a jail term of over 10 years and as a result, the panel finds that he has committed serious crimes in the USA prior to entering Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's four marijuana trafficking offenses cumulatively exceed 10 years jail, constituting serious crimes before Canada entry.

propositions.text: Claimant pleaded guilty voluntarily with counsel; no evidence he was forced or innocent.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that he pleaded guilty to the charges against him. There is no persuasive documentary evidence before the panel to suggest that the claimant was forced to plead guilty. He was represented by a counsel and hence he had an opportunity to establish his innocence if he felt he was innocent. He did not. There is no documentary evidence before the panel from the USA judiciary to suggest that he was not guilty of the drug-related crimes he was convicted for in the USA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant pleaded guilty voluntarily with counsel and no evidence suggests innocence or coercion.

propositions.text: No evidence rebuts presumption of fair US judiciary; claimant convicted and sentenced fairly; lost US permanent resident status and was deported.
propositions.quote: At the hearing, since the claimant did not provide any documentary evidence to rebut the presumption of a fair and independent judiciary process in the USA, the panel finds that the claimant was convicted and sentenced for the crimes he committed in the USA. Since the USA is a functioning democracy, the panel does not believe that the claimant failed to receive a fair hearing conducted by a fair and independent judicial system in the USA. As a result of the criminal convictions, the claimant lost his Permanent Residence status in the USA and was deported to Albania by the USA authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant received a fair US trial, was convicted, lost US status, and was deported.

propositions.text: Claimant committed serious non-political crimes in USA before Canada entry; no evidence crimes were political; sentence completion irrelevant to exclusion validity.
propositions.quote: Based on the evidence adduced, the panel finds that the claimant committed serious, non-political crimes while he was in the USA prior to entering Canada. Since there is no evidence that he committed those crimes for political reasons, the panel finds that the claimant has committed serious non-political crimes outside Canada. The issue as to whether the claimant has completely served his sentence is not determinative as to the legal validity of his exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the United Nations Convention to the status of the refugees, since the Federal Court of Appeal has indicated that exclusion was a possibility even when a sentence was served.9

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant committed serious non-political crimes before Canada entry; sentence completion does not affect exclusion validity.

propositions.text: To rebut presumption of seriousness, claimant must show elements, mode of prosecution, penalty, facts, mitigating/aggravating circumstances
propositions.quote: In Jayasekara,10 in order to rebut the presumption of "seriousness" of the crime the claimant is required to demonstrate with respect to the element of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed and the facts and the mitigating and aggravated circumstances underlying the conviction, as to why exclusion should not apply to him/her.

paragraphs.summary: The prior case Jayasekara requires claimant to rebut seriousness presumption by showing elements, prosecution mode, penalty, facts, and circumstances, court states.

propositions.text: Claimant was adult when committing serious non-political crimes in USA
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant was an adult when he committed the serious non-political crimes in the USA.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows claimant committed serious non-political crimes and was fairly convicted in USA
propositions.quote: documentary evidence11 indicates that the claimant committed the serious non-political crimes in the USA and was convicted by a fair judiciary in USA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant was adult and fairly convicted of serious non-political crimes in USA based on documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant had legal counsel before conviction in USA
propositions.quote: based on the claimant's testimony, he had the benefit of a legal counsel before he was found guilty of the crimes he committed in the USA.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence claimant was innocent or wrongly prosecuted/convicted
propositions.quote: There is no persuasive documentary evidence that suggests that he was innocent and was prosecuted and/or convicted in error.

propositions.text: Mode of prosecution in USA was fair and judicious
propositions.quote: Therefore, the panel finds that the mode of prosecution in the USA was fair and judicious.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant had legal counsel, no evidence of wrongful conviction, and prosecution mode was fair in USA.

propositions.text: Claimant received sentences per USA Criminal Code; deportation and loss of PR status show gravity
propositions.quote: the claimant received sentences in accordance with the USA Criminal Code. His deportation and the loss of his Permanent Resident status in the USA indicate the gravity of the offences he committed.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence of unfair conviction or mitigating/aggravating circumstances
propositions.quote: Since there is no persuasive evidence that the claimant's conviction was in any way unfair, the panel does not find that there were mitigating and aggravating circumstance underlying his conviction.

propositions.text: No evidence crimes were committed for political purpose; crimes were non-political
propositions.quote: Since there is no persuasive evidence to suggest that the claimant's criminal activities in the USA were committed for political purpose, the panel finds that the crimes he committed were "non-political".

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's sentences lawful, no unfairness or mitigating factors, and crimes were non-political.

propositions.text: Claimant committed serious, non-political crimes in USA before coming to Canada
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant committed serious, non-political crimes in the USA before coming to Canada

propositions.text: Individuals who committed serious, non-political crimes outside Canada do not deserve refugee protection in Canada
propositions.quote: individuals like the claimant who have committed serious, non-political crimes outside Canada do not deserve refugee protection in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant committed serious non-political crimes and such individuals do not deserve refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant is excludable under Article 1F(b) of Refugee Convention
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant is excludable because he falls within the parameters of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: Refugee Protection Division excludes claimant for refugee protection
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division excludes XXXXX for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes claimant is excludable under Article 1F(b) and excludes him from refugee protection.
